title: Quant Research Workbench
summary: My private Python workbench for intraday futures research and backtesting, with a public case study on funded-account rules.
question: What happens to a promising backtest when trades get worse prices or cost more to place?
deck: I built a private Python workbench to backtest intraday futures strategies. The funded-account comparison is one example of how I use it.

symbol.name: alpha
symbol.meaning: the edge a strategy claims before costs and fills test it.

figure.alt: Expected net value per simulated account lifecycle was $2,509.22 at baseline, $2,324.31 with an extra $1 per trade, $2,120.10 with an extra $2 per trade, and $888.29 under the 5% fill stress scenario.
figure.caption: The 5% fill stress scenario models worse execution and cuts expected net value from $2,509 to $888 over the simulated life of an account. Adding $2 in fees per trade brings it to $2,120.

sections.title: The workbench
sections.text: I started studying NQ and ES futures on my own in 2021. I built the workbench to turn historical market data into trade setups I could backtest and compare under different rules. The public demo starts with an anonymized trade export and includes selected results and code to analyze them.

sections.title: Checking the trade results
sections.text: For this study, I locked in a benchmark of 1,123 historical out-of-sample trades before comparing it with more recent windows. I resampled trades within each window to estimate how uncertain its average profit or loss per trade was.

figure.alt: All five evaluation windows have positive estimates of dollars per trade. The bootstrap intervals for the 20-, 30-, and 60-session windows cross zero. The intervals for the 45- and 90-session windows stay above zero.
figure.caption: Dots show average P&L per trade. Lines show bootstrap intervals. Three of the five intervals cross zero, even though all five averages are positive.

sections.title: Same trades, different account rules
sections.text: I used Monte Carlo simulations to see how the same trade history would fare under five sets of account rules. Drawdown limits, fees, and payout terms changed the net result, even with the underlying trades held fixed.

figure.alt: Expected net value for the same trades ranged from a loss of $165.65 under MyFundedFutures Flex 50K to a gain of $3,740.59 under MyFundedFutures Rapid 50K. The other three account programs were positive.
figure.caption: Average simulated outcomes ranged from a loss of about $166 to a gain of about $3,741 per account.

sections.title: What I carried forward
sections.text: A filter that kept only volatile sessions had the highest simulated account value among three rules I compared. Its interval for average profit per trade crossed zero. I kept the only rule whose interval stayed above zero for further evaluation. These results use historical trades and simulated execution. I’d need live fills to tell how well they carry over.
